questions.question: The Königsberg bridge problem asks whether a closed walk can cross each of the city's seven bridges exactly once. How is the city turned into a network?
options: Each bridge is a vertex, linked to the regions it touches.
Each land region becomes a vertex and each bridge an edge.
Each pair of regions joined by bridges becomes one edge.
Each region becomes a vertex, joined by edges weighted by distance.

questions.question: In Königsberg, land regions $A$ (the island), $B$, $C$ and $D$ are linked by seven bridges: two between $A$ and $B$, two between $A$ and $C$, and one each between $A$ and $D$, $B$ and $D$, $C$ and $D$. How should the two bridges between $A$ and $B$ be represented in the network?
options: As one edge, since they join the same regions.
As one edge of weight 2, counting both bridges.
As two separate edges, both joining $A$ and $B$.
As no edge, since parallel bridges cancel out.

questions.question: The Königsberg bridge problem asks for a walk that crosses each of the seven bridges exactly once. Which further requirement is part of the problem?
options: The walk must end in the same region where it started.
The walk must visit every land region exactly once.
The walk may end anywhere, as only bridges matter.
The walk must start on the island, the central region.

questions.question: For the Königsberg bridge problem (a closed walk crossing each of seven bridges exactly once), why is a vertex-degree argument better than trying out walks?
options: It finds a valid walk faster than trying walks by hand.
It rules out all walks at once, however many there are.
It is only an estimate; trying all walks is the real proof.
It applies only to the specific layout of Königsberg.

questions.question: To answer the Königsberg question (a closed walk crossing each of seven bridges exactly once), which information about the city is needed?
options: The length of each bridge in metres.
The exact position of each bridge along the banks.
Which pair of regions each bridge connects.
The land area of each region.

questions.question: In Königsberg, land regions $A$ (the island), $B$, $C$ and $D$ are linked by seven bridges: two between $A$ and $B$, two between $A$ and $C$, and one each between $A$ and $D$, $B$ and $D$, $C$ and $D$. What are the degrees of $A$, $B$, $C$ and $D$ in the network?
In a bridge network, every land region is a vertex and every bridge an edge. The four regions have degrees 5, 3, 3 and 3. How many bridges are there?

In Königsberg, land regions $A$ (the island), $B$, $C$ and $D$ are linked by seven bridges: two between $A$ and $B$, two between $A$ and $C$, and one each between $A$ and $D$, $B$ and $D$, $C$ and $D$. A new bridge between $B$ and $C$ is built. Can a closed walk now cross each of the eight bridges exactly once?
options: Yes; $B$ and $C$ now have even degree 4.
No; but only because $D$ has odd degree.
Yes, if the walk starts on the island $A$.
No; $A$ and $D$ are still odd (5 and 3).

questions.question: In Königsberg, land regions $A$ (the island), $B$, $C$ and $D$ are linked by seven bridges: two between $A$ and $B$, two between $A$ and $C$, and one each between $A$ and $D$, $B$ and $D$, $C$ and $D$. The bridge between $A$ and $D$ is removed. Which regions then have odd degree?
options: $A$ and $D$
$B$ and $C$
All four regions
No region

questions.question: Another city has regions $X$, $Y$, $Z$, with two bridges between each pair of regions (six bridges in total). Can a closed walk cross each bridge exactly once?
options: No; using both bridges between two regions repeats a crossing.
No; at least four regions are needed for such a walk.
Yes; the walk X-Y-Z-X-Y-Z-X uses each of the bridges once.
No; each region has degree 4, which rules the walk out.

questions.question: In Königsberg, land regions $A$ (the island), $B$, $C$ and $D$ are linked by seven bridges: two between $A$ and $B$, two between $A$ and $C$, and one each between $A$ and $D$, $B$ and $D$, $C$ and $D$. The walker no longer needs to return to the starting region. Can a walk cross each bridge exactly once?
options: Yes; only the return to the start was impossible.
No; such a walk has at most two odd-degree regions.
Yes, if it starts at $A$, which has the most bridges.
Yes, as three odd regions are allowed in an open walk.

questions.question: In Königsberg, land regions $A$ (the island), $B$, $C$ and $D$ are linked by seven bridges: two between $A$ and $B$, two between $A$ and $C$, and one each between $A$ and $D$, $B$ and $D$, $C$ and $D$. A student draws a single edge for each pair of regions joined by bridges, so $A\text{-}B$ and $A\text{-}C$ appear once each. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing; merging parallel bridges keeps the answer the same.
The degrees all become even, wrongly suggesting a closed walk.
Only edge lengths change; the degrees stay 5, 3, 3, 3.
The degrees become 3, 2, 2, 3, which misrepresents the city.

questions.question: For a closed walk that crosses every bridge of a city exactly once, why must even the starting region have an even number of bridges?
options: It need not; the starting region may have odd degree.
Its first departure pairs with the walk's final arrival.
It needs exactly one bridge, used to leave and return.
The start is ignored, since the walk begins there.

questions.question: In Königsberg, land regions $A$ (the island), $B$, $C$ and $D$ are linked by seven bridges: two between $A$ and $B$, two between $A$ and $C$, and one each between $A$ and $D$, $B$ and $D$, $C$ and $D$. A visitor wants to start on bank $B$, finish on bank $C$ and cross each bridge exactly once. Is this possible?
options: Yes; $B$ and $C$ are odd, so they suit the two ends.
Yes, by passing through the island $A$ several times.
No, but only because $A$ has an odd degree.
No; $A$ and $D$ would also need even degree.

questions.question: In Königsberg, land regions $A$ (the island), $B$, $C$ and $D$ are linked by seven bridges: two between $A$ and $B$, two between $A$ and $C$, and one each between $A$ and $D$, $B$ and $D$, $C$ and $D$. The bridge between $B$ and $D$ is destroyed. A walker wants to cross each remaining bridge exactly once, not necessarily returning. Between which regions must the walk run?
options: From $A$ to $C$, or from $C$ to $A$
From $B$ to $D$, or from $D$ to $B$
Between any two regions the walker chooses
From $A$ to $D$, or from $D$ to $A$

questions.question: A city has regions $P,Q,R,S,T$ and bridges $P\text{-}Q$, $Q\text{-}R$, $R\text{-}S$, $S\text{-}T$, $T\text{-}P$, $P\text{-}R$ and $R\text{-}T$. Can a closed walk cross each bridge exactly once?
options: Yes; region $R$ has even degree 4.
No; region $R$ has degree 4, the most.
No; regions $Q$ and $S$ have only two bridges.
No; regions $P$ and $T$ have odd degree 3.

questions.question: After rebuilding, a planner claims that exactly one land region of a city has an odd number of bridges. Bridges join two different regions. What follows?
options: The claim is wrong: odd regions come in even numbers.
Then a closed walk crossing every bridge once exists.
Then a walk crossing every bridge once must start there.
The claim is possible if that region has many bridges.

questions.question: In Königsberg, land regions $A$ (the island), $B$, $C$ and $D$ are linked by seven bridges: two between $A$ and $B$, two between $A$ and $C$, and one each between $A$ and $D$, $B$ and $D$, $C$ and $D$. Why can no single new bridge make a closed walk across every bridge possible?
options: It can, if the new bridge joins two odd regions.
It can, if the new bridge joins the island to a bank.
One bridge fixes the parity of two regions; four are odd.
It can, if the new bridge is long enough to skip a region.

questions.question: In Königsberg, land regions $A$ (the island), $B$, $C$ and $D$ are linked by seven bridges: two between $A$ and $B$, two between $A$ and $C$, and one each between $A$ and $D$, $B$ and $D$, $C$ and $D$. A tourist must return to the start and may cross exactly one bridge twice, crossing every other bridge exactly once. Can such a walk exist?
options: Yes, by crossing one of the $A\text{-}B$ bridges twice.
Yes, by crossing the $A\text{-}D$ bridge twice.
No; crossing a bridge twice fixes only two odd regions.
Yes, as a repeated crossing removes every parity obstacle.

questions.question: In Königsberg, land regions $A$ (the island), $B$, $C$ and $D$ are linked by seven bridges: two between $A$ and $B$, two between $A$ and $C$, and one each between $A$ and $D$, $B$ and $D$, $C$ and $D$. Two new bridges are to be built so that a closed walk can cross every bridge, old and new, exactly once. Which pair of new bridges achieves this?
options: Two new bridges at A, to B and to C
A new A-B bridge plus a new B-C bridge
Two new bridges at B, to C and to D
A new A-D bridge plus a new B-C bridge
